subject: Intent Statement
comment: The proposed intent statement is unnecessary and ill conceived. The potential for unintended consequences is enormous. Consider a few scenarios. 1. An owner determines to subdivide his farmland, make necessary infrastructure improvements and sell the individual lots. He is not a builder, but will simply sell the lots and allow the purchasers to design and build their own homes, thus avoiding a "cookie cutter" development. How would that happen under the proposed intent statement? If 10 of the 100 lots have to be something other than single family homes, how is that determined? Can he sell the first 90 and hope someone comes along wanting to build some other housing type on the remaining 10? And what if no one does? Do the 10 lots just sit unsold? Or would he be required to sell 1 of every 10 for a non-single family home before he can sell the 11th lot? What if 9 sell and no one buys the 10th for a diﬀerent housing type? Do the other 9 lots sit unoccupied for perhaps years? Or would this mean no landowner could ever just sell empty lots? 2. What happens in the scenario of a predominantly single-family-detached subdivision where an obligatory "other" housing-type structure burns down or is destroyed by some other means. If it were a mansion-style 4-plex, for example, could anything other than a mansion-style 4-plex be built to replace it? Would some sort of restriction be placed on that lot that would forever run with the land? Could it be replaced with 6 attached townhomes (assuming the subdivision would still not exceed density), or something else as long as it isn't single-family- detached? Could that really be controlled a couple of decades after the original development? These are just a couple of questions that have arisen in my mind, but I am confident that there are many, many more troublesome scenarios waiting to rear their ugly heads. I would like to know if any municipality in Utah has adopted such a scheme as that contemplated in the proposed intent statement. Or is this just one person's idea, and southwest Provo will be the guinea pig to see what happens? The far superior, and much less problematic approach is to apply a variety of housing types to the southwest quadrant as a whole, and adopt the planning map created by the committee. That map has the overwhelming support of residents, matches density with infrastructure, and is a proven method of accomplishing the desired objective. - Rick Smith

subject: west side plan
comment: Do you mind including my thoughts in your presentation to the planning commission? I would like to start out with what I see as a bonus for this proposal. As you all know 2 of the plans that were presented were actually in my neighborhood. The town home project that was approved and the other one with the mixture of housing types that still needs to go through planning commission. Even though I was not a part of the committee that formed the map I did sit down with Bill and I was under the understanding that 3 different housing types were to be in these ldr nodes. This was to be a part of the written portion of the master plan that still is not completed. The developer did put in 3 different types of townhomes but it was not what was discussed as what would be apart of these ldr nodes. Housing types like what Harding proposed was along the lines of what we had discussed and what was expected. I am supportive of what Harding is trying to accomplish. The ldr node was NOT very supported by the residents of the neighborhood. I feel like something along the lines that Harding proposed would be more heavily supported by the neighborhood. It is more of what we have been telling them is coming. I am glad you are hashing this out because without the written portion of the master plan I feel like this is a good move and wish that it had been implemented earlier. With that said I do have some concerns with how it currently sits. I like the hypothesis of having mixed housing types within a development, however I question the practicality of it. I was told by a planner that developers usually only have a few product types they produce. You would need a developer as big as Horton is in order to achieve that vision. I am afraid that we are setting ourselves up for some unintended consequences by not looking into this further. I would hate to put us in a position where smaller developers cannot do projects in west Provo because they cannot afford to purchase additional architectural plans and/or have desires to hold onto properties for rentals. I would also hate for this to be a DR Horton monopoly on building in SW Provo. I feel like there is a lot to be said about having different developers come in and create their vision. I also look at the desires for some of my land owners for their properties. I have one family that would like to subdivide their farm land amongst their children. They would each get a portion for their home and some to farm. The idea of being forced to do varying lot sizes and hold onto a portion for rental property does NOT fit into their plans nor intentions for their property nor does that meet the intent of the committee in the guiding principals of allowing farming to continue for as long as they would like. I would like to see some flexibility in these guidelines. I am not sure how to fix that, but maybe a set acreage may be a good compromise? Such as developments within the res zones must meet this criteria if the development is 15 acres or larger? I do not know, just throwing that number out there. Also, I understand the desire to provide housing for teachers, police officers as well as fire fighters within the south west area. My husband is an elementary school teacher and I am a stay at home mom that volunteers as a neighborhood chair for Provo. We live in Lakewood because that is where we could find "affordable housing". Of course, we could have moved further south where we could afford a bigger home for the same price we paid for ours in Provo, but we, unlike some of his colleagues, decided we did not want the travel time. Those in the same boat as us have all bought starter homes here in Provo and as their families grow they move out of Provo to get the bigger homes that are available in Orem or other areas. This same issue of people buying starter homes here in South West Provo and then moving on to a different municipality has been an issue for years. The existing homes here; for the most part, are small. People on the west side have been asking and even begging for larger homes for years. In Lakewood, as well as other south west neighborhoods, the price of our homes...including the one I currently live in today, cost less then a townhome. These are very "affordable" units but admittedly they are a different product then the townhome where they do have a yard and no HOA fees. These are so affordable that we even have police officers and firefighters that live amongst us teachers here in south west Provo. I was speaking with a Provo police officer last week and he was saying that he and 6 other police officers live in the same vicinity of Spanish Fork. I do NOT think that is because there is a lack of housing units here in Provo, because my friend, Provo Animal Control Officer, Jacob Wilson, purchased a home in the Fort Utah Neighborhood just a few years ago. I do believe this has more to do with you can get more home for a cheaper price in the southern part of the county than you can here. I believe just like we are seeing with the teachers, it is a matter of priorities and choice rather than available stock or product. When looking at the south west side of Provo, I ask you to look at all of it and see how to balance that out along with what future development will hold. I hear a lot that the poverty rate here in Provo is due to the students. I always ask that they look harder to see what is here and what we see. If it is cheap enough for the students, it is also cheap enough for those of us who need affordable housing as well. If we look at demographics, west side kiddos are amongst those in poverty along with those downtown neighborhoods that are around us. While we do have some students...not a lot, but some...we do have some great families, individuals, people who are just struggling to survive and Provo provides those housing options for us. Please consider everything while weighing your decisions. Thanks for your time. Becky Bogdin

subject: Email for the planning commission
comment: We are against the proposal of mixed housing everywhere. That is a bad idea and not fair to the citizens who built in an area because they wanted the specific zone that existed at the time--such as single family residential or residential/agricultural. I’ve lived in townhomes and apartments—they have their place— and we specifically moved to the area to get away from higher density. And now we have two city council members pushing their agenda that is overwhelmingly disliked by the current neighborhood and citizens of the area, and trying to force everywhere to be mixed. Who thought this was a good idea? Provo should have mixed housing, and it can be mixed with certain areas being a certain way. But to make everywhere the same is ludicrous and damaging to the current residents. These two city council members seem to be on the younger side and are very verbal in comparison to the other members. I feel that the older members are tired and just defer to these two, and are letting them make a lot of decisions because it’s easy. It seems that we are not being protected by the city council, based on how they routinely ask these two for information/opinions to form their own. Housing should match the surrounding neighborhoods, and be conducive to the area. Also, the idea of mixed housing everywhere seems very communistic. It’s experimental and I have not seen it done. We don’t want a community like Vineyard. I wish our city council was more like Alpine's or Highland’s, where their standards are higher. It also seems very odd that these two council members would push so hard for an entitled, experimental idea. Why would these city council members be against a developer’s proposal of single family homes when it fits everything in the west side plan? These two want to interpret the plan and change it so it fits their agenda. Is there some sort of hidden, non-altruistic motivation? Why fight so hard for an idea so universally opposed? Also, didn’t mayor Kaufusi want to preserve the agricultural feel of this area? Single family homes are hard to come by, especially in Provo. The developer of the Lakeshore Drive proposal says that these will be million dollar homes. If you add mixed homes in the neighborhood, that won’t appeal to prospective buyers of those million dollar homes. They will take their investment and tax dollars elsewhere where they are more protected. It also does not appeal to the surrounding neighborhoods or existing landowners/homeowners. It lowers property values, and increases congestion in the streets with more traffic and parked cars--leading to crime and safety problems. Existing water and sewage issues are only made more challenging with higher densities. And finally, current Center Street traffic is already near capacity. Increasing traffic would likely lead to eminent domain takings of existing Center Street properties, costing millions of taxpayer dollars.

subject: E-Mail for the Planning Commission
comment: Hi Jonathon, Here's an e-mail for the planning commission: Dear Planning Commission, My name is Christian vom Lehn and I am a resident of the Fort Utah Neighborhood. I am writing to comment on the upcoming review of the Future Land Use Intent Statement for the Southwest Area of Provo. I have already commented a few times on this matter, online to the planning commission and via e-mail to the City Council. With the recent discussion that took place in the City Council meeting on June 15, I wanted to add a few additional comments. As I understand it, the core issue at stake with this future land use intent statement is the interpretation of points 3a-3d in the Westside Development policies. The land use intent statement seeks to articulate more specific language about what these points mean, establishing more specific guidelines for what a "mix of housing types" means and the exact degree of granularity to which these policies apply (proposed is all residential developments greater than 10 acres). My previous comments have primarily focused on the concerning process by which this land use intent statement has been drafted. In contrast to the long, deliberate, inclusive process by which the original Westside Development policies have been crafted, this land use intent statement was originally drafted quickly and without input from local stakeholders (and not brought to their attention until observant residents flagged this item on the City Council agenda). It was also drafted knowing well that it ran contrary to the desires of local stakeholders. I still have these concerns. This statement feels rushed and imprecise, something that has already been realized in the significant revisions that have taken place since its initial announcement. For these reasons alone, I oppose the statement, believing that a longer, more thorough process should be taken here (once that I suspect would not result in a very watered down version of the statement being accepted, if accepted at all). I do appreciate the City Council's desire to see a more thorough process and get more input by referring this issue to the planning commission. With signs of improvement in the process, I wish to add a few comments on the merits of the proposed statement. The short version of my additional comment is this -- I sympathize with the desired goals of the statement, but the policies proposed to achieve those goals are problematic. As I see it, the proponents of this statement feel that the primary objections to the statement (and mixed/high density housing at large) stem from NIMBYism ("Not in My Backyard"). This is a common issue in urban planning and one I am very sympathetic to. I am generally in favor of alternative housing types, even in my own neighborhood (and even in my own backyard, but I do not reside adjacent to the remaining properties to be developed). But it seems like the proposed solution to fight perceived "Not in My Backyard" sentiments is a policy of "In Everyone's Backyard." Obviously, that is a bit of an oversimplification, given that the statement only requires 10% of new developments to be alternative housing types. But I believe that "In Everyone's Backyard" is very much the spirit of the proposal. "In Everyone's Backyard" is a policy that doesn't provide much wiggle room. Already, significant flags have been raised about how this policy will lead to unintended consequences. The statement had to be revised to acknowledge that developments less than 10 acres would face problems meeting this standard. What about developments of 11 acres? 15 acres? The threshold established seems arbitrary at best. Notably, the developer from D.R. Horton who commented at the City Council meeting (on June 15) flagged that something like 40-50 acres was the minimum development size they thought would be needed to implement the proposed policies in the land use intent statement. Concerns were also raised that many developers would be excluded from building under these guidelines. Do we really want to privilege certain developers over others as a matter of policy? Do we really want to make it more difficult to develop land in Provo? Further, do we really want to provide incentives for land owners and developers to divide land plots into 10 acre developments to sidestep these policies? Certainly, if we were restarting Provo from scratch today, our new development plans would look very different from how the city is laid out at present. And I believe we should be seeking to appropriately diversify housing options, with more mixed and high density development. And yet, I have not heard a coherent, careful argument for why "In Everyone's Backyard" is the right policy for implementing this vision (the lack of argument may again speak to the rushed nature of the land use statement as well). As it stands, the heart of the argument in favor of the land use statement seems to be "this is what we really agreed upon" and not any attempt to persuade residents of this policy to implement this vision (or address concerns of unintended consequences). This strikes me as a poor motivation for such a potentially restrictive policy. Maybe further study and argument could highlight how this policy would be very beneficial for the city and even the neighborhood. Maybe such arguments were made years ago in the planning stages of the Westside development policies. But since those are long in the rearview mirror, it seems the fight should no longer be about interpretation of a past document, but what is best going forward. And without substantially more effort researching development policies and incorporating feedback from all stakeholders (which perhaps the planning commission is doing), it seems like we are not ready to be making firm policies along the lines of those proposed in the land use intent statement. My recommendation would be that the planning commission recommend the City Council not adopt the land use intent statement, but remain with the existing document. At the very least, I would like to see any future land use intent statement crafted more collaboratively than this one has been. I would also recommend reiterating the vote of support for the proposed development on Lakeshore Drive (as the land use statement appears to have been rushed to get in front of the proposed re-zone on that property). Many thanks for reading this lengthy comment! Best, Christian vom Lehn
